tickets.title: Read a command
tickets.brief:
The terminal hands your program one line at a time: handle(line) gets the text and returns the reply. handle is already written. It answers PING and ECHO. What it needs is tokenize(line), which splits the line into words.

Spaces separate words, except inside double quotes. ECHO "hello world" again is three words: ECHO, hello world and again. The quotes themselves are not part of the word. A quote that never closes is an error: raise ValueError("unclosed quote") and handle turns it into ERR unclosed quote.
tickets.why: Every tool that reads commands starts here: shells, SQL, Redis, git. line.split() looks right until somebody stores a value with a space in it. Walking the line one character at a time, remembering whether you're inside quotes, is the smallest real lexer, and you'll write bigger ones later.
tickets.picture:
ECHO "hello world" again
  └──┘ └───────────┘ └───┘
  word    one word    word

  inside the quotes, a space doesn't split
todo: Keep "quoted text" as one word, without the quotes
"" is a word too: an empty one
Raise ValueError("unclosed quote") for a quote that never closes
tickets.tests:
assert shell.tokenize("SET a 1") == ["SET", "a", "1"], "Plain words split on spaces"
assert shell.tokenize("  GET   a ") == ["GET", "a"], "Extra spaces between words are not words"
assert shell.tokenize('SET greeting "hello world"') == ["SET", "greeting", "hello world"], "A quoted value keeps its space and loses its quotes"
assert shell.tokenize('ECHO ""') == ["ECHO", ""], 'An empty pair of quotes is a word: the empty string'
assert shell.tokenize("") == [], "An empty line has no words"
try:
    shell.tokenize('ECHO "oops')
    unclosed = None
except ValueError as e:
    unclosed = str(e)
assert unclosed == "unclosed quote", 'A quote that never closes should raise ValueError("unclosed quote")'
assert run('ECHO "hello world" again') == "hello world again", "The terminal path works end to end"

A " flips quoted and marks the word as started, but isn't added to it. A space only ends a word when you're not inside quotes.
After the loop: if quoted is still true, raise ValueError("unclosed quote"). If started, append the last word.

tickets.title: Remember things
tickets.brief:
Now Ledger stores data. Add four commands to handle, keeping everything in a dictionary called DATA at the top of shell.py:

CommandReply
SET key valueOK
GET keythe value, or (nil) if there's no such key
DEL key1 if it deleted something, 0 if not
KEYSevery key, sorted, one per line, or (empty)

Commands ignore case (set works), but keys and values don't. A command with the wrong number of words answers ERR wrong number of arguments for 'set', naming the command in lower case.
tickets.why: A protocol is a promise: every command has a fixed shape and one reply. Checking the argument count before doing anything means a typo can never half-run a command. Redis keeps a table of each command's arity for exactly this reason, and so will you.
tickets.picture:
"SET  name  tulip"  ──tokenize──▶  [SET, name, tulip]
                                        │
          ARITY["SET"] == 2 ? ──no──▶ ERR wrong number of arguments for 'set'
                │ yes
          DATA["name"] = "tulip"  ──▶  OK

Check the argument count before running a command
SET, GET, DEL and KEYS, with the replies in the table

tickets.title: Give the data an owner
tickets.brief:
Right now any line of shell.py can reach into DATA. Move the data into its own object: a Store class in a new file, store.py. Its methods are the only way in:

  • set(key, value), get(key) (returns None if missing), delete(key) (returns True if it deleted), keys() (sorted)
  • incr(key): adds 1 to a whole-number value and returns the new number. A missing key counts as 0. If the value isn't a whole number, raise ValueError("value is not an integer").

Then make shell.py use it: from store import Store, one store called db = Store(), and a new command INCR key that answers the new number, or ERR value is not an integer.
tickets.why: This is encapsulation. When the next ticket has to write every change to disk, there will be exactly one place to do it, Store, instead of every command that touches DATA. The shell only speaks; the store owns. Real databases split the same way: a network layer that parses, and a storage engine behind it.
tickets.picture:
shell.py                         store.py
  ┌──────────────┐  db.set(k, v)  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ tokenize     │ ─────────────▶ │ Store            │
  │ handle       │  db.get(k)     │   data = {...}   │  ← nobody else
  │   SET/GET/…  │ ◀───────────── │   set get delete │    touches data
  └──────────────┘                │   keys incr      │
                                  └──────────────────┘

shell.py makes one db = Store() and uses only its methods

tickets.title: Survive a restart
tickets.brief:
Press Restart in the terminal: every key is gone, because data lived in memory. Fix it with an append-only log in a new file, log.py:

  • Log(path) remembers the file name.
  • log.append(record) adds one record, a list like ["SET", "views", "42"], as one line of JSON at the end of the file. Flush it and os.fsync it before returning.
  • log.read() returns every record in the file, oldest first (an empty list if the file doesn't exist yet).

Then Store(log) takes an optional log. When it has one, it replays every record at start-up, and writes each change to the log before changing data. In shell.py, open it as db = Store(Log("ledger.log")).
tickets.why: Memory is fast and forgets. Disk remembers. An append-only log is the simplest way to make a database durable: you never rewrite old bytes, you only add a line, so a write is one quick operation. To rebuild the state, you replay the log from the top. Redis's AOF, Kafka, and the write-ahead log in Postgres and SQLite all start from this idea. fsync matters: without it, "written" can still mean "sitting in the OS's memory".
tickets.picture:
SET a 1   ─▶  ledger.log  ["SET","a","1"]
  SET b 2   ─▶              ["SET","b","2"]
  DEL a     ─▶              ["DEL","a"]
                     │
   restart ──replay top to bottom──▶  data = {"b": "2"}
todo: Log.append writes one JSON line and fsyncs it
Store(log) replays at start-up and logs every change

tickets.title: Pull the plug mid-write
tickets.brief:
Type a few SETs, then press ⚡ Pull the plug. It kills Ledger halfway through writing its last line, the way a power cut would, and starts it again. It won't start: json.loads chokes on half a record.

Make the log crash-safe:

  • Each line becomes crc json: the CRC-32 of the JSON text as 8 hex digits, a space, then the JSON. zlib.crc32(body.encode()) gives the number; f"{n:08x}" formats it.
  • When reading, stop at the first line that is torn: no newline at the end, or a CRC that doesn't match. Every record before it is good.
  • Cut the file back to the end of the last good line, so the next append starts on a clean line instead of being glued onto the garbage.
tickets.why: A disk writes in pieces, and power can go between any two of them. A database has to tell "the last write didn't finish" from "the data is fine", and the only honest answer is a checksum: the record proves itself. Dropping the torn tail is safe because that write was never acknowledged, so nobody was told OK. The cut-back step is the part people forget: without it, the next record is glued to half a line and is lost too.

1c291ca3 ["SET","a","1"]⏎        crc ok   ✓ keep
  a8f0e6b1 ["SET","b","2"]⏎        crc ok   ✓ keep
  5d2c41f0 ["SET","c",            torn     ✗ stop here
                     ▲
       truncate the file to here, then append cleanly
todo: Stop reading at the first torn or damaged line

tickets.title: Keep the log small
tickets.brief:
Run INCR views a thousand times and the log holds a thousand lines, though only the last one matters. Every restart replays them all. Add COMPACT, which rewrites the log as one SET per live key.

  • Store counts the records in its log, count: one per record replayed at start-up, one per record it writes.
  • Log.rewrite(records) replaces the whole file. Write every record to ledger.log.tmp (the log's path plus .tmp), flush and fsync it, then os.replace it over the log.
  • A .tmp file found at start-up is the leftover of a compaction that crashed before its swap. Log(path) removes it.
  • store.compact() rewrites the log from data, keys sorted, and returns (before, after). The shell answers compacted 8 records into 2.
tickets.why: An append-only log only grows. Every log-structured system has to clean up behind itself: Redis rewrites its AOF, Kafka compacts topics, LevelDB and Cassandra merge their files. The dangerous moment is the swap. Writing over the log in place means a crash leaves half a new log and no old one. Writing a copy and renaming it over the original is safe, because a rename is atomic: afterwards the file is either the whole old log or the whole new one.
tickets.picture:
ledger.log (8 lines)        ledger.log.tmp            ledger.log (2 lines)
  SET hits 1                  SET b 2                   SET b 2
  SET hits 2    ──rewrite──▶  SET hits 5   ──replace──▶  SET hits 5
  …                           fsync ✓        (atomic)
  SET b 2
todo: Log.rewrite writes a .tmp copy, fsyncs it, then os.replace

tickets.title: Keys that forget
tickets.brief:
A login session should vanish after an hour, without anyone deleting it. Add two commands:

CommandReply
EXPIRE key seconds1 if the key exists (it now dies after that many seconds), 0 if not. Seconds that aren't a whole number: ERR value is not an integer
TTL keyseconds left, rounded up; -1 for a key with no deadline; -2 for no key
  • Store reads the time only through self.clock, which defaults to time.time. The tests swap it for a fake clock.
  • Log the deadline, ["EXPIRE", key, clock() + seconds], not the duration, so a restart doesn't give the key a fresh hour.
  • A key past its deadline acts as if it isn't there, for GET, KEYS, DEL, INCR and TTL. Writing a new value with SET or INCR clears the deadline.
  • compact() leaves dead keys out, and keeps each live key's deadline as an EXPIRE record after its SET.
tickets.why: Caches, sessions, rate limits and locks all need data that forgets. The trick is lazy expiry: nothing sweeps the database on a timer. Each key carries its deadline, and a read checks it. Redis works this way, plus a slow background sweep for keys nobody reads. Reading time through one clock is how real systems test anything about time: you can't wait an hour in a test, but you can move a fake clock.
tickets.picture:
SET session abc        data    {session: abc}
  EXPIRE session 10      expires {session: 1010}      ← logged as a moment
        clock 1004.5 ─▶  TTL session = ⌈5.5⌉ = 6
        clock 1010   ─▶  GET session = (nil)          ← checked when read
todo: EXPIRE logs the deadline; TTL answers seconds, -1 or -2
Dead keys are invisible to every command
SET clears a deadline; compaction keeps live ones

tickets.title: All or nothing
tickets.brief:
Moving money is two writes: take 10 from one balance, add 10 to the other. Pull the plug between them and the money is gone. Add transactions:

CommandReply
MULTIOK, and start queueing. Inside, MULTI again answers ERR MULTI calls can not be nested
any other command, insideQUEUED. Nothing runs yet, not even reads
EXECrun the queue in order and answer each reply numbered, one per line: 1) OK, 2) 42. An empty queue answers (empty)
DISCARDOK, and drop the queue
  • EXEC or DISCARD outside a transaction: ERR EXEC without MULTI (or DISCARD).
  • A command that's wrong while queueing (unknown, or the wrong number of arguments) answers its error as usual and spoils the transaction: EXEC then answers EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors and runs nothing.
  • The point: the whole transaction is one record in the log, ["TX", [record, record, …]]. Give Store a begin() that starts holding records back and a commit() that writes them as one. A crash tears one line, and with it the whole transaction, so you get all the writes or none.
tickets.why: That's the A in ACID: atomicity. The log from ticket 5 already drops a torn line whole, so wrapping several writes in one line makes them land together for free. Real databases do the same with a commit record: Postgres writes a transaction's changes to its WAL, and only the final commit record makes them count. Queueing first also means a typo in the third command can't leave the first two half-done.

projects.finish: You wrote a database you can talk to. It keeps every write on disk, survives a power cut in the middle of one, cleans up its own log, forgets keys on time, and lands several writes together or not at all. Try it in the terminal: MULTI, two or three SET commands, EXEC, then pull the plug and read them back.
projects.intro:
Ledger is a small database in the spirit of Redis. You talk to it in a terminal. SET stores a value, GET reads it, and it remembers everything even after the program is killed in the middle of a write.

You'll write it in three files, the way a real one is laid out: shell.py speaks the protocol, store.py owns the data and log.py keeps it safe on disk. Every ticket adds one part, and the map on the right lights it up.

tickets.title: Hello, Express
tickets.brief:
Press Run and type GET / in the terminal. The answer is 404 Not Found and Cannot GET /: the server is running, but it has no routes yet, so Express answers for you.

An Express app is a list of routes. app.get(path, handler) says: when a GET request comes in for this path, call handler(req, res). req is the request; res is how you answer. res.send(text) sends the answer and finishes it.

Add two routes:

RequestAnswer
GET /Hello from Express!
GET /abouta sentence about the API that mentions Greenhouse

app.listen(3000) at the bottom starts the server on port 3000, where client.js sends its requests. Try GET / -i once it works, and look at the headers Express added for you.
tickets.why: Every Express app you'll ever read starts with these four lines: create the app, add routes, answer with res.send, listen on a port. The headers you see with -i are Express doing work for you. content-type tells the client it's HTML. etag is a fingerprint of the body, so a browser can ask "has it changed?" instead of downloading it again. x-powered-by just advertises Express; real apps often turn it off with app.disable("x-powered-by").

Inside the handler, res.send("Hello from Express!") is the whole answer.

tickets.title: Send JSON
tickets.brief:
An API answers with data, not sentences, and the format for data on the web is JSON. Give the app some plants, in an array at the top of app.js:

const plants = [
  { id: 1, name: "Tulip", water: "weekly" },
  { id: 2, name: "Fern", water: "daily" },
  { id: 3, name: "Cactus", water: "monthly" },
];

Then add two routes:

  • GET /api/plants answers the whole array with res.json(plants).
  • GET /api/stats answers {"count": 3, "byWater": {"weekly": 1, "daily": 1, "monthly": 1}}: how many plants there are, and how many need each kind of watering. Count them with a loop, so the numbers stay right when plants are added later.
tickets.why: res.json turns the value into JSON text and sets Content-Type: application/json, which is how the client knows to parse it. Putting API routes under /api is a common convention: it keeps data routes apart from pages, and lets you put middleware on all of them at once later. The data lives in memory for now, so it starts fresh every time the server does. Taskflow, the next project, saves it to disk.

For the stats, start with const byWater = {} and, for each plant, byWater[plant.water] = (byWater[plant.water] || 0) + 1.
Then res.json({ count: plants.length, byWater }). Writing { byWater } is short for { byWater: byWater }.

tickets.title: Route parameters
tickets.brief:
GET /api/plants/2 should answer just the Fern. You can't write a route for every id, so Express routes can have parameters: in /api/plants/:id, the :id part matches any value, and the handler finds it in req.params.id.

Add:

  • GET /api/plants/:id: the plant with that id. If there isn't one, answer 404 with {"error": "Plant not found"}: res.status(404).json(...).
  • GET /hello/:name: answers Hello, Ada! for /hello/Ada.

Careful: req.params.id is always a string, "2", while the ids in your array are numbers. Turn it into a number before you compare.
tickets.why: Paths that name a thing, /api/plants/2, are the heart of REST: every resource has its own URL. The status code is part of the answer, not decoration. A client checks for 404 before it reads the body, so a missing plant must never come back as 200 with an empty body. And the string-versus-number trap is real: "2" === 2 is false, so find quietly finds nothing.

plants.find((p) => p.id === Number(req.params.id)) gives the plant, or undefined.
if (!plant) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Plant not found" }); The return matters: without it, the handler carries on and tries to answer twice.

tickets.title: Query strings
tickets.brief:
Lists need filters. The part of a URL after ? is the query string, and Express parses it into req.query: for /api/plants?water=weekly&sort=name, req.query is { water: "weekly", sort: "name" }.

Make GET /api/plants understand three optional filters, in any combination:

QueryKeeps
?water=weeklyplants with exactly that watering
?search=cplants whose name contains the text, ignoring case
?sort=nameall of them, sorted by name A to Z

With no query at all, it's the whole list in its usual order, as before.
tickets.why: Filtering in the query string, not in the path, is the REST convention: /api/plants is still the one collection, and the query only narrows the view of it. Every filter is optional, so the code starts from the whole list and narrows it one step at a time. Sort a copy ([...result]): sort changes the array in place, and sorting plants itself would quietly reorder your data for every later request.

tickets.title: Create with POST
tickets.brief:
Now clients can add plants. POST /api/plants {"name": "Rose", "water": "weekly"} sends the new plant as JSON in the request body. Express doesn't read bodies until you ask: add app.use(express.json()) near the top, and the parsed body appears in req.body.

Add POST /api/plants:

  • Check the body before trusting it. If name isn't a non-empty string, answer 400 {"error": "name is required"}. If water isn't daily, weekly or monthly, answer 400 {"error": "water must be daily, weekly or monthly"}.
  • Otherwise make the plant with the next id (4, then 5…) and the name trimmed, add it to plants, and answer 201 Created with the plant and a Location header: /api/plants/4. res.status(201).location(url).json(plant) does all three.

A request with no body at all leaves req.body undefined, so read it as req.body || {}.
tickets.why: Never trust the body. Anything can arrive: a missing field, a number where a string should be, a script. Checking it first, and answering 400 with a message that says what's wrong, is the most important habit in backend work. 201 plus Location is how HTTP says "created, and here's where it lives", so a client can fetch it next without guessing the URL.
todo: 400 for a missing name, or a watering that isn't one of the three
201 with the plant and a Location header

const { name, water } = req.body || {}; Then typeof name !== "string" || !name.trim() catches missing, wrong-typed and blank names in one check.
Keep let nextId = 4; beside the array, and const WATER = ["daily", "weekly", "monthly"] so you can ask WATER.includes(water).

tickets.title: Update and delete
tickets.brief:
Finish CRUD: create, read, update, delete. HTTP has two ways to update:

  • PUT /api/plants/:id replaces the plant: the body must be a whole valid plant, name and water. Answer 200 with the updated plant.
  • PATCH /api/plants/:id changes only the fields it sends: {"water": "daily"} keeps the name. Check only the fields that are there.
  • DELETE /api/plants/:id removes it and answers 204 No Content: res.status(204).end().

All three answer the same 404 {"error": "Plant not found"} for a plant that isn't there. Both updates answer the same 400s as POST.

POST, PUT and PATCH now check the same things, so write the checks once, in a function problem(body, partial) that returns the error message, or null if the body is fine. With partial, it only checks fields that are present.
tickets.why: PUT and PATCH look alike but promise different things. PUT sends the whole thing, so sending it twice leaves the same result: that's called idempotent, and it means a client can safely retry it after a timeout. PATCH sends a change. 204 is the honest answer to a delete: it worked, and there's nothing left to show. Writing validation once means the three routes can never drift apart, like one accepting a watering of hourly that the others refuse.

In problem, if (!partial || "name" in body) means: check the name unless this is a PATCH that didn't send one.

tickets.title: Middleware
tickets.brief:
Look at the five plant routes: most of them start with the same three lines to find the plant, and three repeat the same checks. Express's answer to repeated code is middleware: a function (req, res, next) that does one job, then calls next() to hand the request on, or answers and stops.

Refactor with three of them:

  • A logger, added with app.use before everything: when each response finishes (res.on("finish", ...)), console.log the method, URL and status, like GET /api/plants/1 200. Use req.originalUrl.
  • findPlant: loads the plant named by :id into req.plant, or answers the 404. Put it in front of every /:id route: app.get("/api/plants/:id", findPlant, (req, res) => res.json(req.plant)).
  • validate(partial): returns a middleware that answers the 400 if problem(...) finds one. validate(false) for POST and PUT, validate(true) for PATCH.

Nothing a client sees changes, except the log lines in the terminal. That's what a refactor is.
tickets.why: A route with a chain of middleware reads like a sentence: find the plant, validate the body, then update it. Each piece is small, named and reusable, and the same idea gives you auth (requireLogin), rate limits and caching later, as one more function in the chain. The order matters: middleware runs in the order you add it, so the logger goes first, and findPlant comes before validate, so a missing plant is a 404 whatever its body says.
tickets.picture:
PATCH /api/plants/2
    logger ── next() ──▶ express.json ── next() ──▶ findPlant ── next() ──▶ validate(true) ── next() ──▶ handler
                                                     │ no plant              │ bad body
                                                     └─▶ 404                 └─▶ 400
hints: The logger: app.use((req, res, next) => { res.on("finish", () => console.log(...)); next(); }); It has to call next(), or every request stops there.
findPlant(req, res, next) sets req.plant, answers the 404 if it's missing, and otherwise calls next(). The route handlers then use req.plant.
validate returns a function: function validate(partial) { return (req, res, next) => { ... }; }. That's a middleware factory, the same shape as express.json().

tickets.title: Errors, the Express way
tickets.brief:
Three things still go wrong in ways a client can't use:

  • POST /api/plants {"name": (broken JSON) gets Express's default 400 page, as plain text, in the middle of a JSON API.
  • GET /api/nothing gets Cannot GET /api/nothing, also plain text.
  • GET /api/plants/abc says Plant not found, when the real problem is that abc isn't an id at all.

Fix them with Express's error handling:

  1. Write httpError(status, message): it makes an Error with a status property. Now middleware can throw httpError(404, "Plant not found") instead of answering itself. Make findPlant throw 400 "id must be a number" for an id that isn't digits, and the 404 for a missing plant. Make validate throw its 400.
  2. After all the routes, app.use("/api", ...) answers anything left under /api with 404 {"error": "No such route: GET /api/nothing"}.
  3. Last of all, an error handler: a middleware with four arguments, (err, req, res, next). Express skips ordinary routes and sends every error here. Broken JSON comes with err.type === "entity.parse.failed": answer 400 {"error": "Invalid JSON"}. Otherwise answer err.status with {"error": err.message}, or for anything without a status, 500 {"error": "Something went wrong"}, logged with console.error.

Then add one async route, the kind real apps are full of. GET /api/plants/:id/tip awaits careTip(water), a function that pretends to call another service, and answers {"plant": "Cactus", "tip": "..."}.
tickets.why: Throwing lets the code that finds the problem stop right there, and lets one place, the error handler, decide what every error looks like. That's how real APIs stay consistent. The 500 message is deliberately vague: the client can't fix your bug, and details like stack traces and SQL tell attackers about your internals, so they go to your logs instead. Express 5 also catches errors from async handlers, which Express 4 didn't. That's why careTip can fail without taking the server down.

findPlant ── throw httpError(400, "id must be a number") ──┐
  validate  ── throw httpError(400, "name is required") ─────┤ Express skips ordinary
  express.json ── broken JSON (err.type) ────────────────────┤ routes, straight to
  async route ── a rejected promise ─────────────────────────┘ (err, req, res, next)
                                                                  └─▶ {"error": ...} + status

projects.finish: You built a REST API in Express, the way they're built at work: routes and params, query filters, all four of create, read, update and delete, validation as reusable middleware, and errors that always come back as JSON with the right status. Every request in this project answers exactly as it does on the real Express 5: tools/wb-express-parity.js replays each terminal session on both, line for line. Next, Taskflow keeps its data on disk and serves a page of its own.
projects.intro:
This is the project people build when they learn Express: a small REST API, grown one feature at a time. It's about plants, so every request reads like something real: GET /api/plants?water=weekly, POST /api/plants {"name": "Rose", "water": "weekly"}.

Express is the web framework most Node backends use, and the sandbox has it built in: require("express") works with nothing to install. The terminal is a client: client.js starts your server, then sends each line you type as a real HTTP request. Add -i to any request to see the response headers too.

tickets.title: A task list
tickets.brief:
The starting code has what you built in Greenhouse: express.json(), httpError(status, message), a problem(body, partial) that checks a task, and an error handler that answers every error as JSON. A task looks like this:

{ id: 1, title: "Buy bulbs", priority: "normal", done: false }

Add the first routes:

  • GET /api/tasks: every task, as a JSON array.
  • GET /api/tasks/:id: one task. Write a middleware findTask that puts it in req.task, or throws httpError(404, "Task not found").
  • POST /api/tasks: check the body with problem, and throw a 400 if it fails. Then make a task with the next id, the title trimmed, the priority it was sent ("normal" if none) and done: false. Answer 201 with a Location header.
tickets.why: It's the same shape as Greenhouse on purpose: most APIs are a collection, one item by id, and a way to add. Starting from code that's already right, instead of a blank file, is what joining a real codebase is like. A new task decides its own done: false. Never let a client set fields it shouldn't control on creation, like an id or a status.
hints: function findTask(req, res, next) { req.task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === Number(req.params.id)); if (!req.task) throw httpError(404, "Task not found"); next(); }
In POST: const body = req.body || {}; const bad = problem(body); if (bad) throw httpError(400, bad);
const task = { id: nextId++, title: body.title.trim(), priority: body.priority || "normal", done: false };, then push it and res.status(201).location("/api/tasks/" + task.id).json(task).

tickets.title: Tick it off
tickets.brief:
A todo list is for ticking things off. Add:

  • PATCH /api/tasks/:id: change only the fields that were sent, title (trimmed), priority and done. Check them with problem(body, true) first. {"done": true} ticks a task off; {"done": "yes"} is a 400, because done must be a real true or false.
  • DELETE /api/tasks/:id: remove it and answer 204.

Both use findTask, so a missing task is a 404 for free.
tickets.why: PATCH is the natural verb for "mark this done": the client sends the one field that changed. Checking types strictly matters more than it looks. "false" as a string is truthy in JavaScript, so a filter on if (task.done) would treat it as done. Refusing anything but a real boolean at the door keeps bad data out of the file you're about to start saving.
todo: PATCH changes only the fields it sends

Then one line per field: if ("done" in body) req.task.done = body.done;, and the same for title (trimmed) and priority.
tasks.splice(tasks.indexOf(req.task), 1) removes it; res.status(204).end() answers.

tickets.title: Save to disk
tickets.brief:
Press ↻ restart in the terminal: every task is gone. They only ever lived in memory. Time to keep them in a file.

Write store.js, a small module that owns the file tasks.json:

  • load(): if the file exists, read it and JSON.parse it; if not, return [].
  • save(tasks): write JSON.stringify(tasks) and a newline. Keep it on one line, with no spacing.

Then in app.js, start with const tasks = store.load(), and call store.save(tasks) after every change, before answering. Ids must carry on after a restart: nextId is one more than the highest id loaded, not 1.
tickets.why: Putting all the file handling in one module, behind load and save, means app.js never touches fs. When you swap the file for a real database later, only store.js changes. Saving before answering is a promise: once a client sees 201, the task is on disk. Answer first, crash before the save, and the client was told a lie. The id rule matters too: restart at 1 and you'd hand out an id that's already taken.

app.js                      store.js                  disk
  ──────                      ────────                  ────
  const tasks = store.load()  ─▶ read tasks.json   ◀──  [{"id":1,...},{"id":2,...}]
  POST ─▶ tasks.push(task)
          store.save(tasks)   ─▶ write tasks.json  ──▶  [{"id":1,...},{"id":2,...},{"id":3,...}]

In app.js, const store = require("./store"); and const tasks = store.load();. Put store.save(tasks); in POST, PATCH and DELETE, right before the line that answers.
let nextId = tasks.reduce((max, t) => Math.max(max, t.id), 0) + 1; gives 1 for an empty list.

tickets.title: Atomic saves
tickets.brief:
Add a task, press ⚡ pull the plug, then add another. The power goes out halfway through saving it, and tasks.json is left half-written. Press Run: JSON.parse throws while app.js is loading, so the server can't start at all, and every task that was safely saved is out of reach. One bad moment, and the whole API is down until someone fixes the file by hand.

Fix it twice over in store.js:

  1. Atomic save. Write the new JSON to tasks.json.tmp, then fs.renameSync it over tasks.json. A rename is all or nothing: a power cut leaves the old file or the new one, never half of one. Only the change being saved at that moment is lost.
  2. Safe load. If tasks.json still can't be parsed (a disk error, a bad hand edit), don't crash. Rename it to tasks.json.corrupt so a human can look at it, console.error what happened, and start with [].
tickets.why: This is how real software saves files: editors, databases, package managers and config tools all write a temporary file and rename it. A rename replaces the name in one step, while writing a file takes many. The second fix is about failing safe: a server that refuses to start is down for everyone, while one that sets the bad file aside keeps working and leaves the evidence. Pull the plug again once it's done, and see it hold.

tickets.title: Filters
tickets.brief:
Nobody wants every task every time. Make GET /api/tasks take filters in its query string, in any combination:

QueryKeeps
?done=falseopen tasks (?done=true: finished ones)
?priority=hightasks with that priority
?q=bulbstasks whose title contains the text, ignoring case

req.query.done is a string, "true" or "false". Anything else, like ?done=maybe, is a 400 {"error": "done must be true or false"}.
tickets.why: A filter the server can't apply should be an error, not ignored. If ?done=maybe quietly returned everything, a client with a typo would show finished tasks as open and never know. Query strings only ever carry text, so turning "false" into a real false is the server's job: compare against the string, and never write if (req.query.done), which is true for "false".
tickets.picture:
GET /api/tasks?done=false&priority=high

  tasks ──done === false──▶ open ones ──priority === "high"──▶ res.json(...)
          "false" is a string: compare it as one
hints: Start from let result = tasks; and narrow it only when a filter is present.

For done: if (req.query.done !== undefined) { if (req.query.done !== "true" && req.query.done !== "false") throw httpError(400, ...); result = result.filter((t) => t.done === (req.query.done === "true")); }
For q, lower-case both sides: t.title.toLowerCase().includes(req.query.q.toLowerCase()).

tickets.title: Pages
tickets.brief:
A list of five hundred tasks shouldn't arrive in one answer. Return it a page at a time, with ?page=2&limit=5: page numbers start at 1, limit is 10 if not given, and it's capped at 50, whatever the client asks for.

Keep the answer a plain array, so every client that already reads it keeps working. Put the paging information in headers, as GitHub's API does:

  • X-Total-Count: how many tasks match, across all pages (after filtering).
  • Link: where the other pages are, for example </api/tasks?page=1&limit=5>; rel="prev", </api/tasks?page=3&limit=5>; rel="next". Leave out prev on the first page and next on the last, and leave out the header if there's neither. Keep the other query parameters in the links, so filters carry over: build them from req.query with URLSearchParams, setting page and limit.

?page=0, ?limit=-1 or ?page=two is a 400 {"error": "page and limit must be whole numbers from 1"}. A page past the end is just an empty list.
tickets.why: Paging protects both sides: the server never builds a giant answer, and a phone never downloads one. Putting it in headers instead of changing the body to {"tasks": [...]} is a real design choice: the body stays the same shape, so nothing that already uses it breaks. That kind of backwards compatibility is what makes changing an API safe. Link headers also mean clients follow the URL you give them instead of building their own, so you can change how paging works later.

12 tasks, ?limit=5

  page 1: 1–5     Link: <…page=2&limit=5>; rel="next"
  page 2: 6–10    Link: <…page=1&limit=5>; rel="prev", <…page=3&limit=5>; rel="next"
  page 3: 11–12   Link: <…page=2&limit=5>; rel="prev"
  every page: X-Total-Count: 12

400 for a page or limit that isn't a whole number from 1
A Link header with prev and next, keeping the filters

const size = Math.min(limit, 50), pages = Math.ceil(result.length / size); The page is result.slice((page - 1) size, page size).
A link: const q = new URLSearchParams(req.query); q.set("page", p); q.set("limit", size); return "<" + req.path + "?" + q + '>; rel="next"';. Join the ones that apply with ", ".

tickets.title: Sorting and stats
tickets.brief:
Two more things every list app needs:

  • ?sort=title sorts A to Z, and ?sort=priority puts high first, then normal, then low, keeping ties in id order. Sorting happens after filtering and before paging, so page 2 is page 2 of the sorted list. Sort a copy, never tasks itself.
  • GET /api/stats answers the totals: {"total": 4, "done": 1, "open": 3, "byPriority": {"high": 2, "normal": 1, "low": 1}}.
tickets.why: The order of the steps is the whole lesson: filter, then sort, then page. Page before sorting and every page is sorted on its own, so a high-priority task on page 3 never reaches page 1. Databases follow the same order: WHERE, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT/OFFSET. Priorities sort by a rank ({high: 0, normal: 1, low: 2}), not alphabetically, which would put high before low before normal.
tickets.picture:
GET /api/tasks?done=false&sort=priority&page=2&limit=5

  tasks ─▶ filter (done=false) ─▶ sort (high, normal, low) ─▶ page 2 of 5 ─▶ res.json
           like SQL:  WHERE           ORDER BY                  LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5
hints: const RANK = { high: 0, normal: 1, low: 2 }; then [...result].sort((a, b) => RANK[a.priority] - RANK[b.priority] || a.id - b.id). The || breaks ties.
Put the sort between the filters and the paging code in GET /api/tasks.
Stats: start with const byPriority = { high: 0, normal: 0, low: 0 } and count in a loop. done is tasks.filter((t) => t.done).length.

tickets.title: A page of its own
tickets.brief:
APIs are read by programs, but people like a page. Answer GET / with HTML built from the tasks, the way Express apps did long before front-end frameworks:

<!doctype html><title>Taskflow</title><h1>Taskflow</h1><p>1 of 2 done</p><ul><li class="done normal">Buy bulbs</li>…</ul>

Each task is an <li> whose class is done or open and then its priority. Escape every title before it goes into the HTML. Write escapeHtml(text) to turn &, <, >, " and ' into &, <, >, " and '. Then try adding a task titled <script>alert('hi')</script>.
tickets.why: Without escaping, a task's title becomes part of your page's code. Anyone who can add a task can then run JavaScript in everyone's browser: stealing sessions, posting as them. That's cross-site scripting (XSS), one of the most common security bugs on the web. The rule is simple and absolute: text from users is escaped at the moment it goes into HTML. Template engines like EJS and Pug, and React, do this for you, which is exactly why you should understand what they're doing.

  escaped:  <script>alert('hi')</script>      shown as text, never run
todo: GET / answers an HTML page built from the tasks
hints: const escapeHtml = (s) => String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) => ({ "&": "&", "<": "<", ">": ">", '"': """, "'": "'" })[c]);
Build the items with tasks.map((t) => '<li class="' + (t.done ? "done" : "open") + " " + t.priority + '">' + escapeHtml(t.title) + "</li>").join("").
Then res.send(...) the whole page: res.send labels a string as HTML.

projects.finish: Your API keeps its promises now. Every change is on disk before the client hears OK, a crash mid-save leaves the old file or the new one but never half of one, a bad file is set aside instead of taking the server down, and a long list arrives a page at a time with links to the rest. Every answer matches the real Express 5, line for line. Try pulling the plug in the terminal, then GET /api/tasks. Next, Shortlink turns a long URL into a short one and counts every click.
projects.intro:
Taskflow is the second project people build when they learn Express: a todo API. You've written routes, validation and error handlers in Greenhouse, so they're already in the starting code. This project is about what changes when an API has to keep its data. The data has to survive a restart and a power cut, it has to grow past one screen, and it has to show up safely on a page.

Your tasks live in a file, tasks.json, which you'll see in the Disk panel as it changes. Once there's a file, the terminal grows a ⚡ pull the plug button: it kills the server in the middle of a write, the way a power cut would.

tickets.title: Shorten a link
tickets.brief:
A short code is just a number written in base 62: the digits 0-9, then a-z, then A-Z. Count up from 100000 and every code is three characters, with room for 238,328 links before a fourth character is needed.

In codes.js, write encode(n): take the last digit with n % 62, look it up in DIGITS, put it in front, and divide n by 62 until nothing is left. encode(61) is "Z", encode(62) is "10" and encode(100000) is "q0U".

Then in app.js:

  • checkUrl(url): a 400 "url is required" if it's missing, and a 400 "url must be a full http:// or https:// address" unless new URL(url) parses it and its protocol is http: or https:. Answer u.href, the normalised form.
  • view(link): what clients see, { code, url, short, clicks }, where short is ` ${BASE}/${code} `.
  • POST /api/links {"url": "..."}: make { code: encode(counter++), url, clicks: 0 }, keep it in links by its code, and answer 201 with a Location.
  • GET /api/links/:code: through a findLink middleware, as in Taskflow, with a 404 "Link not found".
tickets.why: A counter can never repeat, so two links can never get the same code, and you never have to check. Base 62 keeps the codes short because every character carries 62 possibilities instead of 10. Random codes are the other choice. They hide how many links you have, but they can collide, so you'd have to check every time. Checking the URL is about safety, not tidiness. A shortener that accepts javascript:alert(1) sends that code to everyone who clicks. Only real web addresses go through.
hints: function encode(n) { let code = ""; do { code = DIGITS[n % 62] + code; n = Math.floor(n / 62); } while (n > 0); return code; }. The do makes encode(0) come out as "0" and not "".
In checkUrl: let u; try { u = new URL(url.trim()); } catch (err) { throw httpError(400, "..."); }, then check u.protocol against "http:" and "https:".
const link = { code: encode(counter++), url, clicks: 0 }; links.set(link.code, link); res.status(201).location("/api/links/" + link.code).json(view(link));

tickets.title: Send them on
tickets.brief:
Now the part people actually use. Add GET /:code: find the link with findLink, then res.redirect(302, url). A browser that gets a 302 goes straight to the Location it names.

After it, add a catch-all, app.use((req, res) => { throw httpError(404, "Not found"); }), so any other path gets a JSON 404 like every other error here.

Try GET /q0U -i to see the whole answer: the status, the Location, and a short text body for clients that don't follow redirects.
tickets.why: Why 302 Found and not 301 Moved Permanently? A browser remembers a 301 and never asks you again: the next click on the same short link goes straight to the long one without touching your server. That's great for speed and terrible for a shortener, because those clicks are invisible to you and you can't change where the link goes. A 302 means "for now, go there", so every click comes back through you. The real shorteners use 301 only when they don't care about counting.

tickets.title: Count the clicks
tickets.brief:
A shortener is mostly a counter. Every time GET /:code redirects, add one to the link's clicks, and one to referrers, keyed by where the click came from.

  • Browsers say where a click came from in the Referer header (spelled that way since 1996). Write source(req): the host of new URL(req.get("Referer")), or "direct" when there's no Referer or it doesn't parse.
  • New links start with referrers: {}, and view shows them.

Only the redirect counts. Reading the stats with GET /api/links/:code isn't a click.

Try it: GET /q0U -H "Referer: https://news.example/item?id=7", then GET /api/links/q0U.
tickets.why: Counting by the host and not the full Referer is on purpose. Full addresses can carry private things, like a search query or an id in a page's URL, and you don't need them to know that a link spread through a news site. A header is input from outside like any other: new URL throws on garbage, and one odd click must never take the redirect down with it. That's why the try is there.
todo: each redirect adds a click, by source

In the redirect: const from = source(req); req.link.clicks++; req.link.referrers[from] = (req.link.referrers[from] || 0) + 1;, then redirect.

tickets.title: Your own alias
tickets.brief:
People want readable links: /spring-sale, not /q0X. Let POST /api/links take an optional alias:

  • It must be 3 to 30 letters, digits or dashes. Anything else is a 400, "alias must be 3 to 30 letters, digits or dashes".
  • api is reserved in any case, because it's your own path: a 400, "api" is reserved (with the alias as sent).
  • If a link already has that code, answer 409 Conflict, "That alias is taken".
  • Otherwise it is the code. Mark the link custom: true.

Here is the trap. Someone can pick the alias q0V, which is a code your counter is about to make. Write freshCode(): take encode(counter++), and keep going while that code is already in links.
tickets.why: 409 Conflict is the status for "your request is fine, but it clashes with what's already here". The client can fix it by picking another name, which is a different situation from a 400. The clash between aliases and generated codes is the classic bug in shorteners. Two ways of making names share one space, and neither knows about the other. You could ban aliases that look like codes, but checking at the one place codes are made is simpler and can't miss a case.
tickets.picture:
POST {"url": ".../a", "alias": "q0V"}  ─▶ q0V taken by an alias
  POST {"url": ".../b"}                  ─▶ freshCode: encode(100000) = q0U, free ─▶ q0U
  POST {"url": ".../c"}                  ─▶ freshCode: q0V taken, skip ─▶ encode(100002) = q0W
hints: Checks go in this order: the format (typeof body.alias !== "string" || !ALIAS.test(body.alias) with const ALIAS = /^[A-Za-z0-9-]{3,30}$/), then reserved, then links.has(body.alias) for the 409.
function freshCode() { let code; do code = encode(counter++); while (links.has(code)); return code; }, and the code is body.alias || freshCode().

tickets.title: One link per URL
tickets.brief:
Shorten the same URL twice and you get two codes, so its clicks are split in two. Fix that with an index: a second Map, byUrl, from each URL to the code made for it.

  • In POST /api/links, a plain request (no alias) for a URL that's already in byUrl gets that link back, with 200 OK and not 201, since nothing was created.
  • A new plain link goes into byUrl too.
  • Asking for an alias always makes a new link, because the client asked for that name.

Since checkUrl answers new URL(url).href, HTTPS://GARDEN.example/tulips and https://garden.example/tulips are the same URL, so they get the same link.
tickets.why: This makes shortening idempotent: sending it twice leaves things as sending it once would. That matters more than it looks. Clients retry when a network blips, and a retried POST that made a second link would quietly split your stats. 200 against 201 tells the client which happened. Normalising before looking up is what makes the index honest. Without it, a capital letter in a host name would count as a different page.

  q0U ─▶ { url: ".../tulips" }            ".../tulips" ─▶ q0U
  tulips ─▶ { url: ".../tulips", custom }   (aliases stay out of the index)

  POST {"url": "HTTPS://GARDEN.example/tulips"}  ─▶ href ".../tulips" ─▶ byUrl ─▶ q0U   200 OK

After links.set(...): if (plain) byUrl.set(url, link.code);

tickets.title: Links that expire
tickets.brief:
A sale link should stop working when the sale ends. Let POST /api/links take an optional ttl, the link's time to live in seconds:

  • It must be a whole number from 1 to 31536000 (a year). Otherwise it's a 400, "ttl must be a whole number of seconds, from 1 to a year".
  • The link gets **expiresAt = Date.now() + ttl * 1000, and view shows expiresIn**: the seconds left, rounded up, and never below 0.
  • Once it has expired, GET /:code answers 410 Gone, "This link has expired", without counting a click. Its stats are still there at /api/links/:code.
  • A link with a ttl is never shared through byUrl. A plain request for the same URL gets a link that doesn't expire.
tickets.why: 410 Gone says something 404 can't: "this was here, and it's gone on purpose". Search engines drop a 410 at once, while they keep retrying a 404 in case it comes back. Storing the moment it expires (expiresAt) is better than storing the ttl, because the check is one comparison and doesn't depend on when the link was made. Showing expiresIn and not the raw timestamp spares the client from trusting its own clock. Keeping expiring links out of the index matters too: hand a permanent link's creator a link that dies tomorrow, and you've broken their poster.
hints: Number.isInteger(body.ttl) is false for "60" and 1.5, which is exactly what you want.
const expired = (link) => !!link.expiresAt && Date.now() >= link.expiresAt;. In the redirect, check it first: if (expired(req.link)) throw httpError(410, "This link has expired");
The dedupe line becomes const plain = body.alias === undefined && body.ttl === undefined;

tickets.title: Keep them
tickets.brief:
Press ↻ restart, and every link is gone. Worse, if you then made a new link, the counter would start at 100000 again and hand out q0U a second time. Anyone holding the old q0U would land on someone else's page.

store.js is started for you. load() reads links.json, or gives { counter: 100000, links: [] }, and sets a damaged file aside, as in Taskflow. Write save(state), atomically: write JSON.stringify(state) and a newline to links.json.tmp, then fs.renameSync it over links.json.

Then in app.js:

  • Start from store.load(). The links Map is built from its links, and counter from its counter.
  • Rebuild byUrl from the loaded links: every link that isn't custom and has no expiresAt.
  • Add persist(), which saves { counter, links: [...links.values()] }. Call it after every change, before answering. A click is a change too.
tickets.why: The counter is the one value that must never go backwards. Losing a link is bad, but reusing a code is worse, because it quietly sends old traffic to a new owner. Saving the counter in the same file as the links, in one atomic write, means a crash can't save one without the other. byUrl isn't saved at all. It's derived from the links, so rebuilding it on start is cheaper than keeping a second copy in step. Saving on every click is one write per visit. That's fine here, and it's the first thing a busy shortener changes, by counting in memory and saving every few seconds.

  POST  ─▶ freshCode() = q0W ─▶ persist() ─▶ .tmp ─▶ rename ─▶ 201
  GET /q0U ─▶ clicks 4 ─▶ persist() ─▶ 302

const saved = store.load(); const links = new Map(saved.links.map((l) => [l.code, l])); let counter = saved.counter;
for (const l of links.values()) if (!l.custom && !l.expiresAt) byUrl.set(l.url, l.code); and const persist = () => store.save({ counter, links: [...links.values()] });

tickets.title: Top links, and tombstones
tickets.brief:
Two last things a real shortener needs.

GET /api/links: the live links, in the order they were made. ?sort=clicks puts the most clicked first, and ?limit= caps how many come back: 10 if it's missing, never more than 100, and a 400 "limit must be a whole number from 1" if it isn't one.

DELETE /api/links/:code: answer 204. Don't remove the code. Replace the link with a tombstone, { code, deleted: true }, and take its URL out of byUrl. A tombstone keeps the code taken forever:

  • GET /:code on a deleted link is 410 Gone, "This link was deleted". The redirect needs its own lookup now, because findLink should treat a tombstone as 404 for the API.
  • freshCode() and the alias check already skip it, because it's still in links.
  • The list leaves tombstones out, and so does rebuilding byUrl.
tickets.why: A short link outlives its database row. It's printed on posters, saved in old emails, and pasted in chat history. If a deleted code could be made again, all of those would start pointing at someone else's page. That's how people get phished through old links. Tombstones are cheap: a code and a flag. The cost is that a deleted alias can't be picked again, and real shorteners accept that. Sorting is stable, so links with the same number of clicks stay in the order they were made.

projects.finish: Your shortener does what the real ones do. A long URL becomes a short code, counted from a number in base 62. Every redirect is a 302, so every click reaches you and is counted by where it came from. People can pick their own alias without ever colliding with a code you'd make. The same URL gives back the same link, a link can expire, and the whole thing survives a restart and a power cut. A deleted code stays a tombstone, so an old link printed on a poster can never lead somewhere new. Every answer matches the real Express 5, line for line. Try POST /api/links {"url": "https://example.com"}, then visit the code it gives you. Next, Inkwell adds accounts: sign-up, hashed passwords and sessions in cookies.
projects.intro:
Shortlink is the third project people build when they learn Express: a URL shortener. You send it a long address and it gives you a short one, like http://localhost:3000/q0U. Anyone who visits the short one is sent on to the long one, and you count every visit.

It looks small, but it's a good tour of real backend questions: how to make short codes that never collide, why the redirect is a 302 and not a 301, how to count clicks, what to do when two people want the same name, and why a deleted link should stay deleted. The routes, the error handler and httpError are the same as in Taskflow, so the new ideas get all the room.

tickets.title: Answer a request
tickets.brief:
Run the project and type GET / in the terminal. Nothing comes back: the server got the request, but nobody answered it.

http.createServer(handler) calls handler(req, res) for every request. req says what was asked: req.method (GET) and req.url (/health). res is how you answer: set res.statusCode, set headers with res.setHeader(name, value), then send the body and finish with res.end(text).

Make the server answer:

RequestStatusBody
GET /200hello from trellis
GET /health200ok
anything else404Not found

Send Content-Type: text/plain with every answer, so the client knows what it got.
tickets.why: Every web framework in every language sits on exactly this: one function that receives every request and must answer each one, exactly once. Express, Fastify, Django and Rails all start here. A request that never gets res.end() hangs until the client gives up, which is one of the most common bugs in real servers. You just saw it from the client's side.
tickets.picture:
client.js                      app.js
  ─────────                      ──────
  GET /health  ──── request ───▶ handler(req, res)
                                   req.method  "GET"
                                   req.url     "/health"
               ◀─── response ───   res.statusCode = 200
  200 OK                           res.setHeader(...)
  ok                               res.end("ok")
todo: Every answer has a Content-Type: text/plain header
tickets.session:
api> GET /
200 OK
hello from trellis
api> GET /health -i
200 OK
content-type: text/plain

ok
api> GET /nope
404 Not Found
Not found
hints: Start with the header, since every answer needs it: res.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/plain") as the first line of the handler.
Then one if per route, checking both req.method === "GET" and req.url === "/". Set res.statusCode, then res.end("...").
The last else is the 404: res.statusCode = 404; res.end("Not found");. Every path through the handler must reach exactly one res.end.

tickets.title: A table of routes
tickets.brief:
One if per route stops working at about the tenth route. Express replaces the chain with a table: app.get("/health", handler) adds a row, and one function looks each request up in it.

Write express() in express.js. It returns app, which is itself a request handler (req, res), so http.createServer(app) works. The app also has:

  • app.get(path, handler), and the same for post, put, patch and delete. Each adds a route and returns app.
  • app.listen(port, callback), which starts an http server that calls app, and returns the server.

A route matches when its method and path both match exactly. The path is req.url without its query string, so /a?x=1 is /a. With no match, answer 404 with Content-Type: text/plain and the body Cannot GET /nope, the method and then the path. Those are Express's own words.

Then rewrite app.js on top of it:

const express = require("./express");
const app = express();
app.get("/", (req, res) => { res.setHeader("Content-Type", "text/plain"); res.end("hello from trellis"); });
// ...and /health the same way
app.listen(3000, () => console.log("listening on http://localhost:3000"));
tickets.why: This is the front controller pattern: one entry point gets every request and dispatches it through a table. Routing becomes data you can add to, list and test, instead of control flow you have to read. Express, Flask, Rails and Spring all have this table at their centre. Returning app from every method is what makes app.get(...).post(...) chain.
tickets.picture:
express.js keeps a table:

     method   path       handler
     ──────   ───────    ───────
     GET      /          hello
     GET      /health    ok

  GET /health?x=1 ─▶ path "/health" ─▶ row 2 ─▶ handler(req, res)
  PUT /health     ─▶ no row          ─▶ 404 "Cannot PUT /health"
todo: app.listen(...) starts a server and returns it

api> GET /
200 OK
hello from trellis
api> DELETE /

Cannot DELETE /
hints: The lookup is one line: routes.find((r) => r.method === req.method && r.path === path), where path is req.url.split("?")[0].
Make the route-adding functions in a loop over METHODS: app[m] = (path, handler) => { routes.push({ method: m.toUpperCase(), path, handler }); return app; }.
app.listen is (...args) => http.createServer(app).listen(...args). server.listen returns the server, so returning its result is enough.

tickets.title: Speak JSON
tickets.brief:
Every handler so far is three lines of setHeader and end. An API answers in JSON almost every time, so Express gives res some helpers. Add them in express.js, on every res before the route runs:

HelperDoes
res.status(code)sets res.statusCode
res.set(name, value)sets a header
res.json(data)sends JSON.stringify(data) with Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
res.send(body)an object goes to res.json; a string is sent as text/html; charset=utf-8

Each returns res, so res.status(201).json(note) chains. A Content-Type the handler set itself wins: only set one if there isn't one yet.

Then give app.js some data. Keep a list of notes in memory, { id: 1, text: "buy tulip bulbs" } and { id: 2, text: "water the trellis" }, and answer GET /notes with all of them. Use res.send for / and /health.
tickets.why: These helpers look like sugar, but they encode rules people get wrong by hand: JSON must be stringified and labelled, or clients mis-read it; the status must be set before the body is sent. Returning res is the fluent interface pattern: each call hands back the object, so a whole answer reads as one sentence.
tickets.picture:
res.status(201).json({ id: 3 })
  └────┬────┘ └───────┬───────┘
   statusCode = 201    Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
   returns res         body '{"id":3}', then res.end
todo: res.send sends strings as HTML and objects as JSON
Don't overwrite a Content-Type that's already set
app.js answers GET /notes with the two notes
tickets.session:
api> GET /notes
200 OK
[{"id":1,"text":"buy tulip bulbs"},{"id":2,"text":"water the trellis"}]
api> GET / -i
200 OK
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8

hello from trellis
hints: Write a function helpers(res) that adds the four methods to res, and call it at the top of app(req, res).
res.json = (data) => { if (!res.getHeader("Content-Type")) res.setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8"); res.end(JSON.stringify(data)); return res; }
In res.send, check body !== null && typeof body === "object" first and hand it to res.json. Arrays are objects too, which is what you want.

tickets.title: Paths with holes
tickets.brief:
GET /notes/2 should be note 2, and you can't add a route for every id. Express routes can have holes: /notes/:id matches /notes/2, and the handler finds "2" in req.params.id.

Turn each route's path into a regular expression when it's added. Each :name becomes ([^/]+), one path segment, and its name goes in a list. /notes/:id becomes /^\/notes\/([^/]+)\/?$/. The \/? lets a trailing slash match too, as in Express. Before a handler runs, set:

  • req.params: each name with its decoded value (a%20b is a b);
  • req.path: the path without the query string;
  • req.query: the query string as an object of strings. new URL(req.url, "http://localhost").searchParams reads it for you.

Then in app.js: GET /notes/:id answers the note, or 404 with {"error": "no such note"}. GET /notes?q=tulip answers only the notes whose text contains q, ignoring case.
tickets.why: Routes compiled to patterns are how every router works, and compiling once when the route is added keeps each request cheap. A param is exactly one segment, because /notes/1/2 should never quietly match /notes/:id. Params and query values are always strings: req.params.id is "2", not 2. Forgetting that is why notes.find((n) => n.id === req.params.id) finds nothing.

app.get("/notes/:id")  ──compile──▶  /^\/notes\/([^/]+)\/?$/   keys: [id]

  GET /notes/2?q=x  ─▶ req.path   "/notes/2"
                       req.params { id: "2" }      a string
                       req.query  { q: "x" }
todo: Compile each route's path to a pattern and a list of param names
Fill req.params, decoded, before the handler runs
GET /notes/:id, with a 404 for a missing note

api> GET /notes/2

Store ...compile(path) on each route. In app, loop over the routes: skip a different method, exec the pattern on req.path, and on a match fill req.params[keys[i]] = decodeURIComponent(m[i + 1]).
In app.js, Number(req.params.id) before comparing with n.id. For search, (req.query.q || "").toLowerCase(), and "".includes is true for every note.

tickets.title: Middleware
tickets.brief:
Some work belongs to many routes: logging every request, checking a key on everything under /admin, loading the note before two different routes use it. Express's answer is its central idea: middleware. A handler gets a third argument, next. It can answer, or call next() to pass the request to the next handler in line.

Rebuild app around one stack of layers, walked by next():

  • app.use(fn) adds a layer that runs for every path. app.use("/admin", fn) runs for /admin and everything under it, but not /administrator.
  • Routes take any number of handlers: app.get("/notes/:id", findNote, show). Each becomes a layer.
  • next() runs the next layer that matches. When there's none left, answer the 404.

Set req.originalUrl = req.url at the start, as Express does. Then in app.js:

  • add a logger, before everything: on the response's "finish" event, console.log the method, original URL and status, like GET /notes/1 → 200;
  • move the note lookup into a middleware findNote that sets req.note or answers the 404, and use it in GET /notes/:id.
tickets.why: Middleware is the chain of responsibility pattern, and it's why Express stayed small: logging, auth, body parsing, compression and CORS are all just layers, written by anyone, in any order. One stack for both middleware and routes keeps the rule simple: layers run in the order you added them. That's why the logger goes first, and why order bugs, like auth added after the route it guards, are real and common.
tickets.picture:
stack:  use(log) ─▶ use("/admin", key) ─▶ get("/notes/:id", findNote) ─▶ get(..., show)

  GET /notes/1
    log          next() ─┐
    /admin? no   skip    │
    findNote  ◀──────────┘ req.note = {...}   next() ─┐
    show      ◀───────────────────────────────────────┘ res.json(req.note)
todo: One stack of layers, walked by next()
The 404 when the stack runs out

api> GET /notes/1

api> GET /notes/9

A prefix pattern ends in (?=/|$) instead of /?$: the path must stop there or go on with a /. Add a second argument to compile, and strip the trailing / first so use("/") matches everything.
app.use(path, ...handlers): if path is a function, it's a handler and the path is "/". In app.js, the logger is res.on("finish", () => console.log(...)); next();.

tickets.title: Read the body
tickets.brief:
Time to write notes. POST /notes {"text": "prune the roses"} sends JSON in the request body, and the body isn't in req yet: it arrives as a stream, in chunks, after your handler starts. You read it with req.on("data", ...) and req.on("end", ...).

Write express.json(), a function that returns a middleware:

  • If the request's Content-Type is application/json (a ; charset=... after it is fine), read the whole body, JSON.parse it into req.body, then call next(). An empty body becomes {}.
  • Anything else: leave req.body alone and call next() straight away.
  • Broken JSON: answer 400 with {"error": "invalid JSON"}.

Then in app.js, app.use(express.json()) and add:

RequestAnswer
POST /notes with a non-empty text201, the new note with the next id and its text trimmed, and a Location: /notes/3 header
POST /notes without one400 {"error": "text is required"}
DELETE /notes/:id204 and no body, or the 404 from findNote
tickets.why: Parsing the body in one middleware, once, means no route ever touches the stream, and every route gets the same rules. Checking Content-Type first stops a form post or a file upload from being fed to JSON.parse. The 201 with a Location header is how HTTP says "made it, and here's where it lives". 204 says "done, nothing to send back". Status codes are part of your API: clients branch on them.
tickets.picture:
POST /notes  Content-Type: application/json
  ├─ chunk  '{"text": "pru'      req.on("data")   raw += chunk
  ├─ chunk  'ne the roses"}'     req.on("data")   raw += chunk
  └─ end                         req.on("end")    req.body = JSON.parse(raw); next()
todo: Only parse application/json, with or without a charset
hints: express.json = function () { return (req, res, next) => { ... }; }. First the type: (req.headers["content-type"] || "").split(";")[0].trim(). Not JSON? return next().
req.setEncoding("utf8") makes each chunk a string. Collect them with req.on("data", (c) => raw += c), and do the parsing in req.on("end", ...), inside a try.
In app.js, check typeof text !== "string" || !text.trim() for the 400. Then res.status(201).set("Location", "/notes/" + note.id).json(note).

tickets.title: Errors don't crash
tickets.brief:
First, see the problem. Add a route to app.js that throws, app.get("/boom", () => { throw new Error("boom"); }), press Run and type GET /boom. The error goes up through your framework, into Node's http server, and nobody catches it, so the whole program dies. Then GET /notes is refused: one bad request took everyone's down. Take the route out again when you've seen it.

Express catches errors and routes them, like requests. Change next in express.js to take an error, next(err):

  • With an error, skip ordinary layers and run only error handlers: functions with four parameters, (err, req, res, next). (handler.length tells you how many a function declares.)
  • Without one, skip the error handlers.
  • Run each handler inside try/catch, and pass what's thrown to next(e). If a handler returns a promise (an async function does), pass its rejection to next too.
  • When the stack runs out with an error nobody handled, answer it: status err.status if it's a 4xx or 5xx, otherwise 500. For a 4xx, send the error's message; for a 500, just Internal Server Error.

express.json() should now call next(err) for broken JSON, with err.status = 400 and the message invalid JSON. In app.js, add an error handler last that answers every error as JSON: {"error": message} with its status, and {"error": "something went wrong"} for a 500.
tickets.why: In Node, an exception nobody catches ends the process, and every request in flight with it. Frameworks turn errors into a second path through the same stack, so one handler at the end decides how errors look. That's also the only safe place to decide what a client may see: a 4xx message helps the client fix its request; a 500's details are your internals, so they stay in your logs. Catching rejected promises is what Express 5 added, because async handlers are now the normal case.
tickets.picture:
layers:   json ─▶ route ─▶ route ─▶ (err, req, res, next) ─▶ final
                       │ throw
                       └──── next(err) ── skips routes ─────▶ handler: res.status(500).json(...)

  no handler at all ───────────────────────────────────────▶ final: 500 "Internal Server Error"
todo: A rejected promise from a handler becomes next(err)
Unhandled errors: 4xx with the message, or 500
app.js: one error handler, last, answering JSON
tickets.session:
api> POST /notes {"text":
POST /notes → 400
400 Bad Request
{"error":"invalid JSON"}
api> GET /notes/1
GET /notes/1 → 200
200 OK
{"id":1,"text":"buy tulip bulbs"}
hints: next(err): inside the loop, if (Boolean(err) !== (layer.handler.length === 4)) continue; skips the wrong kind of layer either way. Then call layer.handler(err, req, res, next) or layer.handler(req, res, next).
Wrap the call: try { const out = ...; if (out && typeof out.then === "function") out.then(null, next); } catch (e) { next(e); }, then return.
After the loop, a done(err, req, res): no error is the 404; otherwise err.status if it's between 400 and 599, else 500, and only a 4xx shows err.message.

tickets.title: Routers
tickets.brief:
app.js is turning into one long file. Real Express apps split routes by resource: notes.js holds everything about notes, written as if it lived at /, and app.js mounts it with app.use("/notes", notes).

Add express.Router(): a router has the same use, get, post, put, patch and delete, and is itself a handler (req, res, next). That one fact makes it mountable. Move the stack and next out of express() into Router(), and make the app a router that also has listen and finishes with done.

When a use layer matches a prefix, the layer sees the request with the prefix cut off:

  • req.url loses it: under /notes, /notes/7?x=1 is /7?x=1 (and /notes alone is /);
  • req.baseUrl gains it: /notes, or /api/users when routers are nested;
  • req.originalUrl never changes.

When the mounted router calls next, put req.url and req.baseUrl back, so the layers after it see the whole path.

Then move the notes routes, findNote and the data into notes.js as a router, and mount it. Build the Location header from req.baseUrl, so notes.js doesn't need to know where it's mounted.
tickets.why: A handler that takes (req, res, next) composes: a router is one, so a router can hold routers, and a whole app can be mounted inside another. That's composition, the same idea as functions calling functions, and it's how big Express codebases stay navigable: one router per resource, each one testable alone. Rewriting the URL on the way in and restoring it on the way out is what lets each router believe it lives at /.

app ─ use("/api") ─▶ api ─ use("/users") ─▶ users ─ get("/:id")

    app     url /api/users/7?x=1    baseUrl ""
    api     url /users/7?x=1        baseUrl /api
    users   url /7?x=1              baseUrl /api/users     params { id: "7" }

A matched prefix moves from req.url to req.baseUrl
Put them back when the router calls next
notes.js is a router, mounted at /notes

In router, save url = req.url and baseUrl = req.baseUrl || "" on the way in. At the top of every next, put them back. When a use layer matches m[0] (like /notes), set req.baseUrl = baseUrl + m[0] and req.url = url.slice(m[0].length), adding a leading / if it's missing.
Recompute req.path from req.url whenever req.url changes, since every layer matches against req.path.

projects.finish: You wrote Express. Not a toy that looks like it, the same shape: express() is a request handler, routes and middleware are one stack walked by next(), errors skip to handlers with four arguments, and routers mount inside routers. Swap your express.js for the real Express 5 and app.js and notes.js run unchanged: tools/wb-express-parity.js replays every terminal session in this project on both, and 13 of 16 answers are identical. The other three differ only where Express adds two headers of its own (an ETag and X-Powered-By) and words a JSON parse error its own way. You'll never wonder what app.use does again.
projects.intro:
Most Node backends are built on Express, and Express is small enough to write yourself in an afternoon. That's what this project is. You start with Node's bare http module, feel what's missing, and add it one piece at a time until you have the same framework: routes, helpers, params, middleware, body parsing, error handling and routers.

The terminal is a client. client.js starts your server, then sends each line you type as a real HTTP request: GET /notes, or POST /notes {"text": "milk"}. Add -i to see the response headers. Your framework goes in express.js, and app.js is a small notes API that uses it exactly the way it would use the real Express.
